html:
Tillya Tepe, "golden hill", is a site in northern Afghanistan where six rich graves held about 20,000 gold ornaments. They date to around the turn of the common era, the 1st century BCE or 1st century CE.

A Soviet and Afghan team led by Viktor Sarianidi found the graves in 1978. Five held women and one a man, probably nomad nobles, perhaps of the Yuezhi or Saka, who ruled Bactria before the rise of the Kushan Empire.

The gold mixes the styles of half the known world:

  • a goddess like the Greek Aphrodite, with wings
  • dragons and animals in the art of the steppe
  • a Chinese mirror and Indian images
  • a Roman coin of the emperor Tiberius

During the wars that followed, the hoard vanished. Many feared it had been looted or melted down. In 2003 it was found intact in a bank vault under the presidential palace in Kabul, where museum staff had hidden it. It has since toured museums around the world.
